title: Where should you look for cost savings across a client's business?
description: Where costs hide (value chain) for case interviews. Use with "How to reduce costs?" to find specific levers in each part of the business.
hook: Look for cost savings by walking along the business from what it buys to how it reaches customers: inputs, operations, people, sales and marketing, distribution and overheads. Then find the biggest cost lines and put a dollar figure on each saving before you recommend anything.
body:
When it helps

Use this checklist inside a cost reduction case, once you know where the cost sits and need specific levers to pull. It also helps in profitability cases when the problem turns out to be on the cost side.

The checklist

Inputs

  • Renegotiate or switch suppliers
  • Buy in bulk or jointly
  • Redesign the input (cheaper materials, fewer variants)

Operations

  • Automate
  • Cut waste and rework
  • Make or outsource (see outsourcing)

People

  • Flexible staffing to match demand
  • Less overtime
  • Fewer management layers

Sales and marketing

  • Cut low-return spend
  • Shift to cheaper channels

Distribution

  • Better routes
  • Renegotiate logistics contracts

Overheads

  • Centralise shared services
  • Property and travel

Start with the biggest lines

Take a regional airline that needs to cut costs by 10%. Walking along the chain gives you fuel (inputs), aircraft turnaround time (operations), crew scheduling (people), travel agent commissions (sales), airport fees (distribution) and head office (overheads). Then ask which lines are biggest. For most airlines, fuel and labour are, so that is where you start. A 10% saving on a line that is 2% of costs barely moves the total.

Put a dollar figure on every idea

An illustrative parcel operator has $100M of annual costs: $45M drivers, $30M transport, $15M sorting and $10M overheads.

  • Route redesign that cuts driver hours by 6% saves 6% × $45M = $2.7M.
  • Fewer empty kilometres, cutting transport costs by 4%, saves 4% × $30M = $1.2M.

Do not just add them to get $3.9M. Better routes cause both savings, so the two estimates may overlap. Check they use the same baseline.

Then compare ideas on annual saving, one-off cost, time to benefit and impact on service. A project that costs $1M and saves $2M a year pays back in six months. That may beat an immediate $500,000 cut that leads to missed deliveries and lost customers. Always protect the metric the client cannot afford to damage.

How it sounds in an interview

"Let me walk along the business from inputs to customers and see where the cost sits. Drivers and transport are 75% of the total, so I'd focus there first. Route redesign could save around $2.7M on drivers alone."

The weak version is "They could automate and renegotiate with suppliers": true of every company and tied to no number.

Common mistakes

  • Listing levers before finding the biggest cost lines.
  • Adding savings that come from the same change.
  • Ignoring one-off costs and service impact.

Practise it

1. A hotel has $20M of annual costs. Staff are 40%, food and drink 20%, energy 10%, and the rest is spread across many small lines. Where do you look first, and what is a 5% staff saving worth?

Show the answer

Staff, at 40% × $20M = $8M, is the biggest line. A 5% saving is 5% × $8M = $400,000 a year, from scheduling staff to match occupancy and cutting overtime. Food and drink ($4M) is next: waste and menu design.

2. A manufacturer says "everything costs too much". What is your first question?

Show the answer

"Could I see the cost base broken down by line, and how each line has changed over the last few years?" You need to know where the money goes, and what has grown fastest, before you pick a lever.
